misconceptionFamilies.label: Representation and translation
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may be selecting or reading the wrong graph, diagram, vector, axis, slope, area, or reference-frame representation.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Name the represented quantity, axes, direction, and relationship before interpreting the representation.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Evidence and measurement
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may be overlooking controls, uncertainty, replication, sensor limits, or the evidence needed to support a claim.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: State the claim, identify the controlled variable, inspect the measurement limits, and name the evidence that would distinguish explanations.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Force and interaction
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may be misidentifying a force, interaction, torque, pressure difference, or acceleration consequence.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Define the system, list the interactions, assign directions, and separate net force or torque from individual forces.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Timing and state
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may be confusing position, speed, velocity, time, period, frequency, or an instantaneous state.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Identify the quantity and time interval, then distinguish its value, rate of change, and sign at the stated instant.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Sign and direction
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may be losing a sign convention, reversing a direction, or treating opposite vectors as unsigned magnitudes.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Choose a positive direction, attach signs before calculating, and report the result with its physical direction.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Quantity and units
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may be confusing related physical quantities or reporting a result with the wrong unit or dimensional meaning.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Name the target quantity, write its defining units, and check that the relationship preserves dimensions.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Equation structure
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may be misapplying an equation through an incorrect factor, ratio, exponent, operation, or variable role.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Write the governing relationship symbolically, isolate the requested variable, then substitute values with units.

misconceptionFamilies.label: System and model boundary

misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: State the system and assumptions, identify external transfers, and name the condition that limits the model.

misconceptionFamilies.label: General reasoning check
misconceptionFamilies.description: The learner may need to restate the target quantity, governing principle, and evidence before choosing among nearby explanations.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Restate what is known, what is requested, and which physical principle connects them before selecting an option.

sections.summary: Force models connect system boundaries, free-body diagrams, Newton laws, gravity, friction, circular motion, and drag.

Residuals can reveal friction, sensor bias, or a changing operating regime.

Remove disagreeing data before checking the apparatus.
Use a conclusion without identifying what measurement supports it.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Evidence-based transfer requires an explicit assumption, a measurable prediction, and uncertainty-aware comparison.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for motion as a model?
flashcards.back: Kinematics represents position, velocity, acceleration, vectors, reference frames, and projectile motion. First move: Choose axes first, then translate between a graph, equation, vector, and verbal claim.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for graph and equation translation?
flashcards.back: Translate slopes, areas, signs, and components before selecting a kinematics equation. First move: Write the representation in words, identify its slope or area, then use the matching relation.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for evidence and model limits?
flashcards.back: Use residuals, controls, and limiting cases to decide whether a motion model remains defensible. First move: State the assumption, predict the observable consequence, and identify evidence that could challenge it.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for forces and interactions?
flashcards.back: Force models connect system boundaries, free-body diagrams, Newton laws, gravity, friction, circular motion, and drag. First move: State the system, draw interactions, choose signs, and then apply Newton second law.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for systems and force diagrams?
flashcards.back: Build a force model from a boundary, interaction list, coordinate axes, and signed component equations. First move: Boundary first, interactions second, axes third, signed Newton equation last.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for friction, drag, and circular evidence?
flashcards.back: Evaluate force models by isolating variables, checking regimes, and comparing measured net effects. First move: Name the regime, identify the controlling variables, and test the model with a measurable net effect.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for energy transfers?
flashcards.back: Work, kinetic energy, gravitational energy, spring energy, and power describe transfers across physical systems. First move: Use a system energy chart before deciding whether a force law or conservation law is more efficient.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for energy accounting routine?
flashcards.back: Choose a system, list energy stores and transfers, and use work or conservation with explicit boundaries. First move: Draw the system energy account first, then select the shortest defensible equation.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for power, efficiency, and model limits?
flashcards.back: Connect energy, time, and useful output while testing where ideal energy models stop matching evidence. First move: Align the interval, convert all quantities to energy, then compare useful transfer with total input.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for momentum and collisions?
flashcards.back: Momentum, impulse, center of mass, and collision models describe short interactions and isolated systems. First move: Write signed momentum terms first, then decide whether kinetic energy is also conserved.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for momentum and impulse representations?
flashcards.back: Use signed momentum, force-time area, and system boundaries to model short interactions. First move: Set the axis, draw the system, integrate the force pulse, and compare total signed momentum.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for collision evidence and system limits?
flashcards.back: Separate conservation claims from measurement limits, deformation, sound, and external impulse. First move: State the conservation law, state its conditions, and name the measurement that tests those conditions.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for torque and rotation?
flashcards.back: Rotational kinematics, torque, rotational inertia, equilibrium, and angular momentum extend force reasoning to rigid bodies. First move: Draw the lever arm, choose a pivot, and keep angular signs consistent.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for torque and equilibrium diagrams?
flashcards.back: Represent lines of action, lever arms, and separate translational and rotational balance conditions. First move: Mark the pivot, draw the perpendicular lever arm, choose signs, and check both equilibrium equations.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for rotational motion and mass distribution?
flashcards.back: Connect angular speed, rotational inertia, and angular momentum when a system changes shape or radius. First move: Name the axis, identify the mass distribution, then choose a kinematic, energy, or momentum relation.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for rotating systems?
flashcards.back: Rolling, rotational energy, angular impulse, and angular-momentum conservation connect rotation to system energy. First move: Use both translation and rotation terms whenever a rigid body rolls.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for rolling energy routine?
flashcards.back: Track translational and rotational kinetic energy together for rolling objects. First move: Write the no-slip relation first, then include both energy forms and any measured loss.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for angular impulse and conservation?
flashcards.back: Use torque-time area and angular momentum to analyze brief pushes and isolated shape changes. First move: Choose the axis, identify torque sources, integrate or conserve angular momentum, then check units.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for oscillations?
flashcards.back: Oscillation models describe restoring forces, period, frequency, phase, and energy exchange. First move: Locate equilibrium and turning points on the graph before applying a timing or energy relationship.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for period, phase, and graph reading?
flashcards.back: Read equilibrium, turning points, slopes, phase, period, and frequency from oscillator graphs. First move: Label equilibrium and turning points before interpreting slope, timing, or energy.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for energy, damping, and evidence?
flashcards.back: Use energy exchange and repeated timing data to distinguish ideal oscillation from damping and apparatus limits. First move: Separate timing evidence from amplitude evidence and test each claim with repeated measurements.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for fluids and conservation?
flashcards.back: Density, pressure, buoyancy, continuity, and Bernoulli reasoning describe stationary and flowing fluids. First move: Identify whether the fluid is stationary or flowing before choosing hydrostatic, continuity, or Bernoulli reasoning.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for density, pressure, and buoyancy?
flashcards.back: Connect microscopic density to pressure forces and buoyant equilibrium without confusing force with pressure. First move: Identify the fluid, depth, displaced volume, and force balance before choosing a pressure relation.

flashcards.front: What is the key move for flow, continuity, and assumptions?
flashcards.back: Use continuity and Bernoulli reasoning only after checking steady, incompressible, and low-loss assumptions. First move: Classify the flow first, state assumptions second, then select conservation relations and test residuals.

diagramPlacements.title: Motion-representation bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Place one motion event into a coordinate sketch, position-time graph, and velocity-time interpretation.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build a three-panel representation for a cart that starts at a positive position, moves in the positive direction, and then slows to rest.
constructionSteps: Draw the axis and mark the initial position.
Sketch position versus time with slope changes that match the verbal motion.
Add a velocity sign or slope annotation for each interval.
Check that the graph reaches zero velocity at the stated stopping event.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: The cart begins to the right of the origin, has positive velocity, and follows a position curve whose positive slope decreases to zero at the stopping time.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: The cart begins to the right of the origin, has positive velocity, and follows a position curve whose positive slope decreases to zero at the stopping time.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: A position value above zero is not enough to determine the sign of velocity; inspect slope.

diagramPlacements.title: Interaction-to-force bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Make the selected system and external interactions visible before writing Newton equations.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build a free-body representation for a block pulled across a rough horizontal surface while a small drag force opposes motion.
constructionSteps: Circle the object included in the system.
Draw only interactions crossing the boundary.
Choose positive axes and resolve angled forces if present.
Add a net-force statement and mark the constant-speed condition if applicable.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: The isolated block has upward normal force, downward weight, a forward applied force, and backward resistive forces; constant speed means their signed net force is zero.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: The isolated block has upward normal force, downward weight, a forward applied force, and backward resistive forces; constant speed means their signed net force is zero.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: Do not add a separate centripetal or motion arrow unless a physical interaction produces it.

diagramPlacements.title: Energy-accounting bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Track energy stores and transfers across a clearly named system boundary.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build an energy representation for a cart released by a spring that rises on a rough ramp and warms the contact surface.
constructionSteps: Name the system and decide whether the ramp surface is inside it.
Draw initial and final energy bars.
Add arrows for work or thermal transfer across the boundary.
Check that the total account closes even if mechanical energy changes.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: Spring energy decreases while gravitational and possibly kinetic energy increase; the rough contact adds thermal energy, so mechanical energy alone need not remain constant.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: Spring energy decreases while gravitational and possibly kinetic energy increase; the rough contact adds thermal energy, so mechanical energy alone need not remain constant.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: A missing thermal or external-work arrow can make a correct conservation claim look falsely violated.

diagramPlacements.title: Collision-before-and-after bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Preserve signed velocity and system membership through a short collision interval.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build before-and-after momentum representations for two carts that approach, collide, and separate with one cart reversing direction.
constructionSteps: Set one positive direction for both snapshots.
Draw velocity arrows with lengths or labels that preserve sign.
Group both carts if testing total momentum conservation.
Compare total signed momentum and separately compare kinetic energy.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: The two-cart system has signed momentum before and after contact; a reversed cart changes sign, while deformation may reduce total kinetic energy without destroying momentum.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: The two-cart system has signed momentum before and after contact; a reversed cart changes sign, while deformation may reduce total kinetic energy without destroying momentum.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: A rebound velocity cannot be represented by a positive speed alone.

diagramPlacements.title: Torque-line-of-action bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Expose the perpendicular lever arm and rotational sign before summing torques.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build a torque representation for a beam with a hanging load and a support force about a chosen pivot.
constructionSteps: Mark the pivot and every force application point.
Extend each force line of action.
Draw the perpendicular distance from pivot to each line.
Sum signed torques, then identify the separate net-force check.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: Torque magnitude equals force times perpendicular distance to the line of action; a force through the pivot has zero torque about that pivot.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: Torque magnitude equals force times perpendicular distance to the line of action; a force through the pivot has zero torque about that pivot.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: The full distance to the force location is not always the lever arm.

diagramPlacements.title: Rolling-energy bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Show that a rolling object has simultaneous center-of-mass translation and rotation.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build a linked representation for a rigid disk rolling without slipping down a ramp.
constructionSteps: Draw the center-of-mass velocity along the ramp.
Mark the angular-velocity direction about the center.
Annotate v equals r omega for no slip.
Split the kinetic-energy account into translational and rotational terms.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: The disk translates down the ramp while rotating about its center; no slipping links center speed to angular speed, and inertia determines energy partition.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: The disk translates down the ramp while rotating about its center; no slipping links center speed to angular speed, and inertia determines energy partition.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: The contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the surface in the ideal no-slip model, not sliding forward.

diagramPlacements.title: Oscillation-phase bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Align displacement, velocity direction, and energy changes over one oscillator cycle.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build a cycle map for a mass-spring oscillator beginning at maximum positive displacement and moving toward equilibrium.
constructionSteps: Mark the positive and negative turning points.
Place equilibrium between them.
Use the displacement slope or motion arrow to infer velocity direction.
Annotate where speed and kinetic energy are largest.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: At maximum positive displacement the mass is momentarily at rest; moving toward equilibrium gives negative displacement slope or leftward velocity, and kinetic energy grows as spring potential energy falls.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: At maximum positive displacement the mass is momentarily at rest; moving toward equilibrium gives negative displacement slope or leftward velocity, and kinetic energy grows as spring potential energy falls.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: Maximum displacement and maximum speed occur at different locations in the ideal cycle.

diagramPlacements.title: Fluid-depth-and-flow bridge
diagramPlacements.purpose: Keep hydrostatic depth reasoning separate from continuity and Bernoulli reasoning in a pipe.
diagramPlacements.prompt: Build a two-part fluid representation: pressure at two depths in a tank and speed-pressure changes in a narrowing pipe.
constructionSteps: Mark equal-depth points in the stationary tank.
Show deeper points with greater gauge pressure.
Draw wide and narrow pipe sections with flow direction.
Annotate the area-speed relationship and any elevation or loss assumption.
diagramPlacements.textEquivalent: In the stationary tank, pressure increases with depth; in steady incompressible flow, a narrower section has greater speed, while pressure also depends on elevation and energy-loss assumptions.
diagramPlacements.altText: Text-first visual scaffold: In the stationary tank, pressure increases with depth; in steady incompressible flow, a narrower section has greater speed, while pressure also depends on elevation and energy-loss assumptions.
diagramPlacements.visualErrorCheck: A narrow pipe does not by itself guarantee higher pressure; classify the model and compare all relevant terms.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Kinematics model-and-evidence brief
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: A cart travels along a marked track while a motion sensor records position at equal time intervals. The class is deciding whether a constant-acceleration model remains defensible after the cart reaches the end of the track.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Construct a short evidence-backed model for the cart. Make each claim traceable to a representation or measurement.

parts.task: Define the positive direction and translate the position record into a velocity or acceleration representation.
parts.lookFor: A stated axis and a correct slope, derivative, or finite-difference interpretation.

parts.task: Use the model to predict one later position or velocity and show the units in the calculation.
parts.lookFor: A named relationship, substituted quantities, and a unit-consistent prediction.

parts.task: Describe one residual pattern that would challenge constant acceleration and identify the likely model limit.
parts.lookFor: A comparison between prediction and measurement rather than a claim based on one point.

parts.task: State one controlled follow-up measurement that could distinguish sensor noise from a changing acceleration.
parts.lookFor: Repeated, time-aligned measurements with a variable or condition held fixed.

scoringGuide.evidence: Coordinate convention, interval, and measured quantity are explicit.
The response connects position, velocity, or acceleration without treating them as interchangeable.
The prediction is compared with data and uncertainty or residuals are acknowledged.
The follow-up test changes one defensible condition and states what result would mean.

selfCheck: Did I state the axis before assigning signs?
Did I distinguish position, velocity, and acceleration?
Did I identify evidence that could disconfirm my model?
commonPitfalls: Treating a positive position as proof of positive velocity.
Calling one close data point validation of the entire time interval.
Changing the sensor, interval, and track condition at the same time.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Force-model and regime investigation
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: A student pulls a block across several surfaces with a spring scale and then repeats the trials while the normal force is changed. At higher speeds, a small drag force may also be present.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Build a force model that separates friction, drag, and net-force evidence, then propose a defensible investigation.

parts.task: Draw or describe the system boundary and list the external interactions on the block.
parts.lookFor: A system choice and interaction-based force list rather than arrows based only on motion.

parts.task: Write a signed component relationship for constant-speed motion and explain what it implies about the net force.
parts.lookFor: A zero-net-force condition with directions and a clear regime assumption.

parts.task: Identify the independent variable, control variables, and measured outcome for testing a friction model.
parts.lookFor: Normal force or surface condition is isolated while speed, contact, and measurement procedure are controlled.

parts.task: Explain how a speed-dependent residual would change the model without declaring the data invalid.
parts.lookFor: Drag or another unmodeled interaction is proposed and tied to a measurable pattern.

scoringGuide.evidence: Boundary, contact forces, and possible drag are named consistently.
The equation reflects direction and distinguishes force from acceleration.
The proposed comparison changes one meaningful variable and records repeatable outcomes.
A residual pattern is interpreted as evidence about assumptions.

selfCheck: Did I identify an interaction for every force arrow?
Did I state when constant speed means net force is zero?
Did I separate static and kinetic friction regimes?
commonPitfalls: Adding centripetal or motion forces as extra interactions.
Assuming the normal force always equals the weight.
Changing surface, normal force, and speed together.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Energy-accounting and efficiency brief
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: A cart is released from a spring and climbs a rough ramp. A speed sensor measures the cart at the bottom and top while a thermal sensor records warming of the contact surface.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Use a system energy account to explain the measured outcome and evaluate the efficiency of the transfer.

parts.task: Choose a system and identify the initial and final energy stores plus transfers across the boundary.
parts.lookFor: A boundary that includes the relevant object, Earth, spring, or surface and names thermal transfer when needed.

parts.task: Write an energy relationship that predicts the top speed or height and define every term used.
parts.lookFor: Consistent stores, signs, units, and a distinction between total and mechanical energy.

parts.task: Use the sensor evidence to decide whether mechanical energy is conserved and explain where the difference goes.
parts.lookFor: Measured speed or thermal evidence is connected to a specific transfer rather than energy being destroyed.

parts.task: Design one change that could improve useful output and state the tradeoff it introduces.
parts.lookFor: A targeted change such as surface, spring, or ramp condition with a measurable consequence.

scoringGuide.evidence: The account identifies what is inside the system and tracks initial and final stores.
The relation is dimensionally consistent and includes the relevant thermal or external-work term.
Observed speed and temperature changes support a conservation or loss claim.
A proposed improvement changes a stated factor and anticipates its effect.

selfCheck: Did I name the destination of energy transferred by friction?
Did I distinguish power from total energy?
Did I compare measured and predicted values on the same interval?
commonPitfalls: Writing conservation before choosing the system.
Calling mechanical-energy loss destruction of total energy.
Comparing input energy from one interval with output from another.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Collision and impulse evidence brief
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: Two carts collide on a low-friction track. Motion sensors record velocities before and after contact, and a force sensor records the collision pulse. The carts deform slightly but remain separate.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Evaluate the collision using signed momentum, impulse, and kinetic-energy evidence.

parts.task: Select the collision system and establish a sign convention for the cart velocities.
parts.lookFor: A fixed axis and a system in which internal collision forces can be distinguished from external impulse.

parts.task: Calculate the total momentum change and compare it with the signed force-time area.
parts.lookFor: Momentum and impulse are treated as directed quantities with compatible units.

parts.task: Decide whether kinetic energy is conserved and identify a physical destination for any decrease.
parts.lookFor: Momentum conservation is separated from kinetic-energy conservation and deformation, sound, or thermal transfer is named.

parts.task: Propose one apparatus check if the momentum residual is larger than the stated uncertainty.
parts.lookFor: Track tilt, sensor timing, friction, or unmeasured external force is tested with a targeted comparison.

scoringGuide.evidence: The axis, system, and velocity signs are explicit.
Force-time area and momentum change are compared as vectors or signed components.
Momentum and kinetic-energy claims are evaluated separately.
A residual leads to a plausible apparatus test rather than data deletion.

selfCheck: Did I use velocity rather than speed for momentum?
Did I state the isolation interval?
Did I identify where kinetic energy can transfer?
commonPitfalls: Conserving kinetic energy by default.
Using force peak instead of force-time area for impulse.
Treating one cart as isolated during the collision.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Torque-equilibrium model brief
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: A horizontal beam is supported at two locations and carries a hanging lamp. A student can move the lamp and measure both support forces but is unsure whether one equilibrium equation is enough.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Construct a rotational-equilibrium solution that can be checked with independent force evidence.

parts.task: Choose a pivot and identify the line of action and signed torque for each relevant force.
parts.lookFor: Perpendicular lever arms, a rotational sign convention, and no invented force arrows.

parts.task: Use the torque sum to predict one support force or the lamp position.
parts.lookFor: A complete torque relationship with distances measured from the chosen pivot.

parts.task: Explain why the net-force condition must also be checked.
parts.lookFor: Rotational equilibrium is separated from translational equilibrium.

parts.task: Describe a measurement that would reveal a misidentified center of mass or support location.
parts.lookFor: A repeatable change in position or load tied to a predicted support-force response.

scoringGuide.evidence: The response uses lines of action and perpendicular distances.
The pivot simplifies the equation without hiding a needed force.
Both net torque and net force requirements are named.
A measured support force or shift can test the model.

selfCheck: Did I measure the perpendicular lever arm?
Did I assign torque signs consistently?
Did I check net force after net torque?
commonPitfalls: Using force magnitude as torque.
Assuming zero torque guarantees zero acceleration.
Ignoring the beam’s weight or center of mass.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Rolling-system energy and momentum brief
constructedResponseWorkshops.unitLabel: Unit 6: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: A disk and a hoop with equal mass and radius roll from rest down the same ramp without slipping. A motion sensor measures center-of-mass speed and a rotary sensor measures angular speed.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Explain the different outcomes using linked translational and rotational models, then identify evidence for nonideal losses.

parts.task: Write the no-slip relation and identify the translational and rotational energy terms.
parts.lookFor: The center-of-mass speed, angular speed, radius, and both kinetic-energy contributions are linked.

parts.task: Predict which object reaches the bottom with greater speed and justify the role of rotational inertia.
parts.lookFor: Mass distribution is connected to the fraction of energy in rotation.

parts.task: Use angular-speed and center-of-mass data to test the no-slip assumption.
parts.lookFor: Measured values are compared through v equals r omega with uncertainty or residuals.

parts.task: Identify one external torque or energy-loss mechanism that could explain a speed deficit.
parts.lookFor: Axle friction, rolling resistance, or slipping is paired with a targeted control.

scoringGuide.evidence: Translation and rotation are represented together with a named axis.
The prediction depends on mass distribution, not mass alone.
Sensor data test v equals r omega and energy expectations.
A loss mechanism is connected to an observable signature.

selfCheck: Did I include rotational kinetic energy?
Did I distinguish angular speed from tangential speed?
Did I state whether static friction is assumed non-dissipative?
commonPitfalls: Treating a rolling body as a point mass.
Assuming equal mass and radius means equal rotational inertia.
Calling every friction force an energy loss.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Oscillation phase-and-evidence brief
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: A spring-mass oscillator is recorded with a position sensor while a second sensor estimates velocity. After several cycles, the amplitude decreases but the time between nearby peaks appears stable.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Use graph relationships and repeated measurements to separate phase, period, amplitude, and damping claims.

parts.task: Identify equilibrium and turning points on the position record and infer the sign of velocity between them.
parts.lookFor: Slope-based velocity reasoning with correct turning-point and equilibrium interpretation.

parts.task: Calculate period and frequency from several cycles and state why averaging helps.
parts.lookFor: Time per cycle is distinguished from cycles per time and timing uncertainty is addressed.

parts.task: Use the changing amplitude and stable peak spacing to evaluate the damping claim.
parts.lookFor: Amplitude and period are treated as separate observables.

parts.task: Design a follow-up that tests whether the spring remains in the simple-harmonic regime at larger amplitude.
parts.lookFor: Amplitude is changed while mass, sensor, and timing procedure are controlled.

scoringGuide.evidence: Position, slope, equilibrium, and turning points are not conflated.
Period and frequency are calculated with consistent units and multiple cycles.
Amplitude loss is separated from the period observation.
A controlled amplitude comparison can reveal model limits.

selfCheck: Did I find velocity from slope rather than height?
Did I use seconds per cycle for period?
Did I avoid inferring damping from one noisy peak?
commonPitfalls: Calling maximum displacement maximum speed.
Treating frequency as a time unit.
Changing mass and amplitude together in a period test.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Fluid-statistics and flow model brief
constructedResponseWorkshops.scenario: Water moves steadily through a transparent pipe that narrows and rises slightly. Pressure sensors and a flow meter are available at two locations, while a submerged block is tested in a separate tank.
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Choose and defend the fluid models for the pipe and the submerged block, including the assumptions that make each relationship useful.

parts.task: Classify the tank and pipe situations as stationary or flowing and name the relevant variables.
parts.lookFor: Hydrostatic, continuity, and energy-per-volume reasoning are selected for the correct regime.

parts.task: Use continuity or pressure-depth reasoning to predict one measurable change.
parts.lookFor: Area, speed, depth, density, and units are matched to the chosen relationship.

parts.task: Explain how pressure differences produce buoyant force on the block.
parts.lookFor: Buoyancy is identified as a net pressure-force result and compared with weight when appropriate.

parts.task: Design a check for leakage, viscosity, or unsteady flow if the measured data fail the ideal model.
parts.lookFor: One assumption is isolated and the required pressure, speed, or flow data are named.

scoringGuide.evidence: Stationary-fluid and flowing-fluid models are kept distinct.
A selected equation includes its variables, assumptions, and units.
Pressure differences, displacement, and buoyant force are connected.
A model mismatch leads to a targeted measurement rather than blind substitution.

spacedReviewSchema.description: A local, unscored cadence for revisiting topic evidence after an adaptive repair or advancement decision.

cadenceStages.purpose: Retry the earliest unmet routine while the feedback is fresh.
Recall the model and representation with reduced cueing.
Apply the model under a changed condition or evidence demand.
Revisit the topic inside unit and cumulative mixed practice.

spacedReviewSchema.intervalPolicy: Intervals are suggested local review windows. Assistive pacing, missed days, and learner preference may change the schedule without creating a penalty or readiness inference.
spacedReviewSchema.privacyBoundary: This cadence is an internal study-planning aid only. It does not infer an official score, readiness, college credit, laboratory competence, diagnosis, or safety clearance.

contentMigration.note: All eight unit chapters now include three navigable sections, 24 section-level flashcards, and 24 memory aids with structured examples, boundaries, misconception guidance, worked data, retrieval, and transfer; 39 deterministic topic diagnostic routes now connect each objective to its three-section study sequence, practice-specific item slices, entry checks, reinforcement sets, transfer sets, knowledge checks, and mastery signals; eight unit synthesis routes now aggregate topic order, starter items, mixed-practice sets, bank links, and practice slices; five cumulative review ladders now expose the existing progression from foundation core through translation, synthesis, chained scenarios, and capstone transfer; a nine-family misconception index now links every distractor explanation to a reusable remediation move and the affected topic, unit, and ladder routes; nine structured remediation playbooks now turn those families into recognize-repair-practice-retry-transfer-reflect loops; 15 study-session plans now turn unit, ladder, workshop, and timed-practice assets into bounded execution paths with success criteria and accessibility controls; 39 mastery checkpoints now define the evidence ledger for model-selection, representation-routine, and evidence-transfer states with deterministic next actions; eight original constructed-response workshops now add model-selection, mathematical, evidence, and experimental-design practice, while eight optional visual scaffolds provide original diagrams with text equivalents; independent review remains pending. 39 adaptive review queues now convert each checkpoint condition into three ordered, text-first, unscored next actions; independent review remains pending. Four-stage spaced review plans now add same-day, next-day, three-day, and seven-day retention touchpoints for all 39 topics; independent review remains pending. Four alternate 42-item internal practice forms now provide deterministic form variety with timing, practice, bank, and review metadata; independent review remains pending.
